newsitem.title: FRANCE: Foreign bond buyers return to France, but late.
newsitem.headline: Foreign bond buyers return to France, but late.

text.p: New figures show foreign investors starting to return to the French bond market after a massive purge of holdings earlier in the year but they may have missed out on chances for big gains, analysts said on Friday.
"The large selloff movement is over...but there won't be a massive return. It's too late," said Morgan Stanley's Eric Chaney. "The bargains have been had," said Nomura's Sonja Gibbs.
Finance ministry data released on Friday showed that non- residents were net buyers of French government bonds in September for the first time since November 1995.
Foreigners bought a net 1.89 billion francs of government bonds (OATs) and shorter-dated BTANs in September after selling a net 14.15 billion the previous month.

But net buying for September was still way down on year earlier purchases of 16.96 billion. And figures for the first nine months of 1996 showed net sales of 152.24 billion compared with net purchases of 68.95 billion.

The foreign sell-off was triggered by a transport strike that shut down the country for more than three weeks last December, fears over France's weakening economy and worries it would not hit deficit targets to qualify for monetary union.

But what foreign investors did not reckon on was the solid flow of funds from domestic insurance companies that supported the market and drove the risk premium on 10-year French bonds over their German counterparts to below parity.
"The common refrain was that the foreigners were pulling out. Well the foreigners did pull out and it didn't go down -- thanks to the domestics," said one trader.

Forecasts last December called for the French 10-year spread over Germany to be around 60 to 70 basis points by the end of 1996. Instead, the spread -- which measures the difference in yields -- has turned negative and touched a low of minus 11 basis points on Friday.
"Since the start of this year, insurance companies' buying ...has supported the market," said Marie Owens-Thomsen of BIP.

The trigger for the initial wave of domestic portfolio reallocation away from cash and into bonds this year was the cutting of the interest rate on a popular tax-free savings vehicle Livret A to 3.5 percent from 4.5 percent, she said.
At the start of 1996, some 700 billion francs was on deposit on Livret A accounts and by the end of the year around 80 billion or 11 percent are expected to have been withdrawn.

Chasing higher yields, the French have redirected their savings into home purchase savings schemes and in insurance contracts which feature tax advantages and these funds tend to reinvest in the five to 10 year area of the curve.

Fears that the government would remove some of the tax breaks for investing in life insurance policies, which did not eventually materialise, also prompted a flood of cash into such policies to beat the tax man.
Partly driving the return of foreign investors now is that so many indexed funds are underweight in France, said Gibbs.

Like Morgan Stanley's Chaney, she does not expect non-residents "to come back in droves. But "there is some perception there could be a little bit more to go in Europan bond markets and France being part of the core, if even only by reason of the political will, stands to benefit," she said.
Analysts said the 10-year OAT-bund spread could widen to 15 or possibly 20 basis points in favour of France.
Economists said while France's economic situation was still bleak with record 12.6 percent unemployment, the political will to be part of the single currency eased risks for investors.

President Jacques Chirac on Wednesday strongly reaffirmed France's commitment to monetary union. "Regarding the EMU, Mr Chirac wants it," said Chaney. "The spectrum of a confidence crisis which resulted in high risk premia on French assets has practically vanished."
But Iain Lindsay of Credit Lyonnais said the chief virtue of the French bond market was its defensive quality as it generally outperformed in a falling market.

"The main positive characteristic is clearly not yield as it is lower yielding (than Germany), not currency because it is higher risk, but it is defensive -- in a negative market it will be better performing (than Germany's)."
